<reason>B defended targeted phaseouts with full lifecycle accounting from the opening, rather than retreating to that position. A offered a credible flexibility argument for fees, but its central attacks relied on an unsupported trivial-or-dangerous dichotomy. Most damagingly, A repeatedly converted B's inability to verify a historical assessment into a supposed concession that no assessments ever occurred, even after correction. B's proportionality argument better justified accepting some transition costs without endorsing indiscriminate bans.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B answered the claim that narrow measures are too trivial to justify regulation: removing unnecessary packaging need only justify its own modest adjustment costs, not solve the entire litter problem. Its closing also exposed that fees producing the same packaging changes would not eliminate the transition costs A emphasized.</best_rebuttal>
